scenes.headline: Building CLIs (argparse & click)
scenes.subtitle: Turning scripts into real tools
scenes.narration: Command-line interfaces turn a one-off script into a reusable, parameterized tool that teammates and schedulers can run with predictable, self-documenting arguments.

scenes.headline: Why a real CLI beats sys.argv
items: Automatic help text and usage messages
Type conversion and validation of arguments
Clear separation of options, flags, and positional inputs
scenes.narration: Reaching into sys.argv by hand works for a single argument but quickly becomes brittle and undocumented. A proper CLI framework generates help and usage text for free, so users discover how to run your tool without reading the source. It also converts and validates inputs, catching a bad value at the boundary instead of deep inside your pipeline.

scenes.headline: argparse vs click
scenes.narration: argparse ships with Python itself, so it adds no dependency, but you build the parser imperatively by adding arguments one call at a time. click is a third-party library that uses decorators to attach options directly to your functions, which reads more cleanly and makes nested subcommands almost effortless. Choose argparse when you want zero dependencies, and click when ergonomics and composability matter.

scenes.headline: A CLI with argparse
scenes.code:
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Run the ETL job")
parser.add_argument("source", help="input path")
parser.add_argument("--rows", type=int, default=1000)
parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")

args = parser.parse_args()
run_etl(args.source, args.rows, args.dry_run)
scenes.narration: This parser declares one positional argument for the source path and two options. The rows option is typed as an int with a default, so argparse converts and validates it automatically. The dry-run flag uses store_true, meaning its mere presence sets it to True. After parse_args reads the command line, the neatly typed values flow straight into the ETL function.

scenes.headline: The same CLI in click
scenes.narration: click expresses the same interface declaratively by stacking decorators above the function. Each argument and option becomes a parameter that click parses, converts, and passes in by name. The is_flag option mirrors argparse's store_true, and click generates the help text automatically. The result is a CLI whose definition lives right next to the logic it drives.

scenes.headline: CLI best practices
items: Provide sensible defaults and a --dry-run mode for safety
Return proper exit codes so schedulers detect failures
Support subcommands to group related operations
scenes.narration: Give every option a sensible default and offer a dry-run mode so users can preview destructive actions safely. Return a non-zero exit code on failure, because that is how cron, Airflow, and CI decide whether your job succeeded. As a tool grows, group related actions under subcommands to keep the interface discoverable rather than sprawling.

scenes.text: A good CLI documents itself, validates inputs, and signals success through exit codes — that is what makes a script production-ready.
scenes.narration: Whether you pick argparse or click, a well-built CLI is self-documenting, validates its inputs, and reports success through exit codes. That combination is exactly what turns a personal script into a dependable production tool.
